<reason>B wins by distinguishing scheduling authority from immunity against harmful conduct. A usefully replaced Egyptian consent with neutral determination, but did not establish why binding, prospective drought safeguards require prior authorization of every timetable. B also more convincingly weighed upstream deprivation, exposing A's inadequate treatment of irreversible medical and livelihood losses during compulsory delay.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B directly challenged A's prevention-versus-compensation framing: measurable drought commitments can constrain retention before shortages, while prior agreements also depend on compliance. A's continued description of B's safeguards as merely retrospective did not adequately answer that distinction.</best_rebuttal>
